record.paper_title: Open problems in queueing theory inspired by datacenter computing
record.original_question: Consider the multiserver job queueing model with n servers, First-Come-First-Served scheduling, and classes of jobs where a class-i job simultaneously requests n_i servers and holds them for a service duration S_i. Even in the simplified case where all jobs have the same exponentially distributed service durations, what is the mean response time for systems with more than n = 2 servers?

evidence.quote: In summary, understanding the mean response time for multiserver job systems with more than n = 2 servers is an entirely open problem, even when all jobs have the same exponentially distributed service durations.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a multiserver job queueing system with a fixed number n of identical servers and First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) scheduling. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process and are partitioned into finitely many classes indexed by i = 1, 2, …, K. A class-i job arrives with probability p_i (independently of the past), simultaneously requires exactly n_i of the n servers (1 ≤ n_i ≤ n), and, once it begins service, holds those n_i servers for a service duration S_i. Under FCFS, the head-of-line job waits until n_i servers are simultaneously available, at which point it occupies n_i servers for its entire service duration; jobs behind it in the queue cannot leapfrog ahead. Assume the system is stable. The response time T of a job is the elapsed time from its arrival until its service completion.

Specialize to the case in which every job, regardless of class, has the same service-time distribution S_i = S ~ Exp(μ) (independent across jobs). For each fixed n ≥ 3, determine the mean response time E[T] in closed form (as a function of n, the server-need distribution {(n_i, p_i)}, the arrival rate λ, and μ).
artifact.status_search_result: Exact closed-form expressions for the mean response time of FCFS multiserver job systems with n ≥ 3 servers remain unknown, even when all job classes share a common exponential service-time distribution. Recent work (Hong–Wang 2021 on sharp waiting-time bounds; Grosof–Scully–Harchol-Balter–Scheller-Wolf 2022 on heavy-traffic optimal scheduling; the finite-skip method; and 2025 lower bounds by Wang–Grosof) provides bounds, asymptotic results in heavy traffic, and stability characterizations, but no exact analysis for general n > 2 has appeared. The problem is consistently described as open in the recent literature.

status_evidence.title: Sharp Waiting-Time Bounds for Multiserver Jobs
status_evidence.snippet: Provides bounds rather than exact mean response time for FCFS multiserver job systems.
status_evidence.claim: Only bounds, not exact formulas, are available for mean waiting/response time.

status_evidence.title: Optimal Scheduling in the Multiserver-job Model under Heavy Traffic
status_evidence.snippet: Characterizes mean response time asymptotically as load approaches 1 with n fixed.
status_evidence.claim: Progress is asymptotic (heavy-traffic) rather than exact for general load.

status_evidence.title: The multiserver job queueing model (QUESTA 2022)
status_evidence.snippet: Almost nothing is known about the performance of multiserver job queueing models; stability region only known in special cases.
status_evidence.claim: Performance analysis of the FCFS multiserver job model remains largely open.

status_evidence.title: Novel Lower Bounds on M/G/k Scheduling (2025)
status_evidence.snippet: Recent lower bounds work continues, indicating exact mean response time is still not known.
status_evidence.claim: Active 2025 research still focuses on bounds, supporting that exact analysis remains open.
